statements.status_notes: Spring Data Commons applications may be vulnerable to denial of service through resource exhaustion when attacker-controlled property path strings are passed to MappingContext property path resolution. Specifically, an application is vulnerable when attacker-controlled input is used as a property path string for path resolution, the consuming module or application exposes this resolution to untrusted callers (for example, when using Spring Data REST), and the targeted domain types contain recursive or sufficiently deeply nested property graphs, or attackers can submit a large number of unique invalid paths. Affected versions: Spring Data Commons 4.0.0 through 4.0.5; 3.5.0 through 3.5.11; 3.4.0 through 3.4.14.
statements.impact_statement: The Liquibase CLI contains no Spring code. The scanner reports spring-data-commons from the license-tracking application, a separately started Spring Boot service shipped in 5.x and removed in 6.0.0. Docker images 5.0.0 through 5.2.2 carry it as an unextracted archive under /liquibase/dist (liquibase-license-tracking-1.0.0-beta.tar.gz). The application carries spring-data-commons 3.4.2 in 5.0.0 to 5.0.2, 3.5.5 in 5.0.3, 4.0.2 in 5.1.0, 4.0.4 in 5.1.1 and 4.0.5 in 5.2.0, all in range, and 4.1.0, outside the range, in 5.2.1 and 5.2.2. The vulnerable cache is filled only when a caller passes externally supplied strings to MappingContext.getPersistentPropertyPath(String, ...), as Spring Data REST and store-specific query mappers do. A bytecode scan of the application found no caller of that method outside spring-data-commons itself, and Spring Data REST is not bundled. Its HTTP endpoints accept only fixed JSON request bodies and no sort, filter or property-path parameters.

statements.status_notes: Spring Data's internal property-lookup cache accepts and permanently retains attacker-supplied strings as cache keys, allowing heap exhaustion through repeated requests. Affected applications are those using Spring Data features that forward HTTP-supplied strings to PropertyPath.from without prior filtering, in particular Querydsl web bindings (via QuerydslPredicateArgumentResolver) with the default permit-all visibility, and @ProjectedPayload form-parameter binding (via MapDataBinder). Affected versions: Spring Data Commons 4.0.0 through 4.0.5; 3.5.0 through 3.5.11; 3.4.0 through 3.4.14; 3.3.0 through 3.3.16; 2.7.19 and earlier.
statements.impact_statement: The Liquibase CLI contains no Spring code. The scanner reports spring-data-commons from the license-tracking application, a separately started Spring Boot service shipped in 5.x and removed in 6.0.0. Docker images 5.0.0 through 5.2.2 carry it as an unextracted archive under /liquibase/dist (liquibase-license-tracking-1.0.0-beta.tar.gz). The application carries spring-data-commons 3.4.2 in 5.0.0 to 5.0.2, 3.5.5 in 5.0.3, 4.0.2 in 5.1.0, 4.0.4 in 5.1.1 and 4.0.5 in 5.2.0, all in range, and 4.1.0, outside the range, in 5.2.1 and 5.2.2. The advisory names two routes from HTTP input into the PropertyPath.from cache: Querydsl web bindings and @ProjectedPayload form binding through MapDataBinder. Querydsl is not bundled, so the Querydsl argument resolver is never registered. The application declares no @ProjectedPayload type, and its endpoints bind only concrete JSON request-body classes, with no Sort, Pageable or projection parameters.
